analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices directly with drug manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never received a committee vote or floor action, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, Medicare is banned from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers. This bill would lift that ban and require the health department to negotiate prices for the most expensive drugs seniors use. If negotiation failed, the price would automatically drop to the lowest of several benchmarks, including the median price charged in five other wealthy countries. It would also require drugmakers to pay rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees, and let the government set a drug list that plans must follow.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, particularly the roughly 65 million people in Part D drug plans, would pay less out of pocket for the most expensive prescriptions. Taxpayers would also save, since Medicare covers a large share of those drug costs. Low-income enrollees would get extra protection through mandatory manufacturer rebates.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'non-interference' provision in Medicare law that forbids the government from negotiating drug prices or setting a formulary.

Requires the Health and Human Services Secretary to negotiate Part D drug prices for plan year 2023 onward, prioritizing the highest-cost drugs: the top 40 by total Medicare spending, the 40 with per-beneficiary annual costs above $10,000, and the 20 with the fastest price increases.
If negotiation fails, the drug's price is set to the lowest of three benchmarks, including the median price in Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, and Japan.

Requires drug manufacturers to pay Medicare a rebate for drugs dispensed to low-income enrollees; a manufacturer that declines to sign the rebate agreement would have its drugs excluded from Medicare drug coverage the following year.
Requires every drug plan to have a process letting enrollees request coverage of a drug that is not on the plan's list or is subject to prior authorization or step therapy.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would face government-set and negotiated prices, a fallback pegged in part to prices in five foreign countries, and new rebate obligations tied to Medicaid rebate levels. Medicare drug plans would also take on new reporting duties backed by civil penalties of up to $10,000 per day for late reporting.

drawbacks.text: The fallback provision would let the government mandate a price without agreement, using the median price in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan; the drug industry and its allies have long argued such price-setting reduces revenue available for developing new medicines.
The bill lets the Health and Human Services Secretary set a drug list that private plans must follow, or require changes to their lists, taking formulary decisions away from the plans.
A manufacturer that refuses the rebate agreement would see its drugs excluded from Medicare drug coverage, a penalty that shifts risk onto patients who use that company's drugs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a well-documented problem: Medicare pays more than other wealthy countries' health systems for many of the same drugs because a 2003 law bars the program from negotiating. Its exceptions process protects access for enrollees whose drugs leave a plan's list. The main honest cost is the risk that forced prices and the foreign-price fallback cut manufacturers' revenue over time; how much that would slow new drug development is disputed. On balance the design is strong for patients and taxpayers, and the burden falls on an industry with among the highest profit margins in health care.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced; the committee never scheduled a markup or vote, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on March 23, 2021, with eight Democratic cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
A Senate Health subcommittee held a hearing on primary health and retirement security where the bill's subject matter was discussed, with the hearing printed as S.Hrg. 117-176.
No further action was taken: the bill received no committee markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers avoided a government negotiation mandate, a foreign-price fallback, and new rebate obligations. Medicare drug plans also avoided a federally set drug list. Patients and taxpayers did not get the lower prices the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug manufacturers and Part D plans

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all eight cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-led Finance Committee never brought the bill to a vote.

industries.note: The bill would replace the current ban on Medicare negotiation with required negotiation, a fallback price pegged partly to foreign prices, and Medicaid-level rebates for drugs given to low-income enrollees. Manufacturers' interests run directly against patients here: the industry's revenue depends on Medicare continuing to pay list prices without negotiation.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D drug plans and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: Negotiated lower prices would cut what plans pay for drugs, but the Secretary could set a drug list the plans must follow or force changes to theirs, and plans would face new rebate-reporting duties with civil penalties. On drug prices the plans' interest runs alongside patients', since plans pay part of the drug bill.
